title: Niobium Titanium Nitride as a High Tensile Stress Material for Nanomechanics
authors: Korbinian Rubenbauer, Burak E. Bülbüloglu, Thomas Luschmann, Manuel Müller, Stephan Geprägs, Witlef Wieczorek, Eva M. Weig, Matthias Althammer, Hans Huebl
abstract: Over the past decades, high-coherence mechanical resonators have been continuously pushed to new limits, using techniques such as dissipation dilution and clamp-tapering to enhance their quality factor beyond intrinsic material limitations. Today, these mechanical resonators are often fabricated from silicon-nitride, silicon-carbide or aluminum. Recently, however, interest in novel material platforms has grown, especially those allowing for the integration within superconducting circuits. Among these, superconducting nitrides stand out as particularly promising due to their high transition temperatures compared to elementary superconductors. Here, we introduce them as nanomechanical resonators and report on the fabrication and characterization of highly stressed, doubly clamped niobium titanium nitride (NbTiN) nanostring resonators. Using optical interferometry, we determine the elastic properties and mechanical quality factor from room temperature to 13 K. We observe high tensile stress up to 0.81 GPa along with a Young's modulus of 181 GPa and an intrinsic mechanical quality factor up to 850. With these favorable mechanical properties, NbTiN constitutes a promising material platform for future applications in cavity electro- and nanomechanics.
summary: This work characterizes Niobium Titanium Nitride (NbTiN) as a promising material for advanced nanomechanical resonators intended for use with superconducting circuits. By measuring resonance frequencies using optical interferometry, the authors determined that NbTiN possesses high tensile stress and good mechanical quality factors across relevant cryogenic temperatures. This establishes it as a viable platform for future cavity electro- and nanomechanics applications.
main_problem: The goal is to develop novel, high-performance material platforms for nanomechanical resonators that can be integrated with superconducting circuits.
main_result: Niobium Titanium Nitride (NbTiN) was characterized as a promising material due to its favorable mechanical properties, including high tensile stress ($\sim 0.81 	ext{ GPa}$) and a measurable intrinsic quality factor ($Q_{	ext{intr}}$ up to $850$).
method: Mechanical properties were determined by fabricating doubly clamped nanostrings and measuring their resonance frequencies using optical interferometry across varying temperatures.
model_or_system: The physical system is a thin film of NbTiN used as a nanostring resonator. Analysis involves fitting the measured resonance frequency ($\Omega$) dependence on string length ($l$) or harmonic order ($n$) to extract elastic constants and stress.
key_observables: Tensile stress ($\sigma$), Young's modulus ($E$), intrinsic mechanical quality factor ($Q_{	ext{intr}}$), and thermal expansion coefficient ($\alpha$).
important_parameters: High tensile stress up to $0.81 	ext{ GPa}$; Young's modulus of $\sim 181 	ext{ GPa}$; operating temperature range down to $13 	ext{ K}$.
main_assumptions: The analysis heavily relies on the high tensile stress approximation for relating resonance frequency to mechanical parameters, and comparisons between different fitting models (e.g., fundamental mode vs. higher harmonics) reveal discrepancies.
figures_summary: Figures show SEM images of nanostrings; characterization plots display resonance peaks ($\Omega$ vs $1/l$), the temperature dependence of $\sigma$, $E$, and $Q_{	ext{intr}}$, and comparisons between different fitting models for stress extraction.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the need for new superconducting nanomechanical materials to presenting experimental measurements using optical interferometry. It then details the analysis methods used to extract elastic constants ($\sigma, E$) and quality factors ($Q_{	ext{intr}}$) as functions of temperature and geometry.
why_interesting: While primarily mechanical/materials science, the focus on superconducting integration and high-quality factor resonators makes it relevant to quantum optomechanics and circuit QED platforms where material limitations are key bottlenecks.
